questions.q: The locus of all the points on the curve \(y^2=4 a\left(x+a \sin \frac{x}{a}\right)\) at which the tangent is parallel to \(x\)-axis is:
questions.solution:
We have
\(y^2=4 a\left(x+a \sin \frac{x}{a}\right)\) ...(i)
Differentiating w.r. \(\mathrm{tx}\),
\(2 y \frac{d y}{d x}=4 a\left[1+\cos \frac{x}{a}\right]\)
Since, the tangent is parallel to \(x-\) axis, \(\frac{d y}{d x}=0\) This gives
\(4 a\left(1+\cos \frac{x}{a}\right)=0 \Rightarrow \cos \frac{x}{a}=-1 \Rightarrow \sin \frac{x}{a}=0\)
\(\therefore\) From (i) \(y^2=4 a(x+0) \Rightarrow y^2=4 a x\), which is the required locus.

questions.q: If the system of equations \(x+\lambda y+2=0\), \(\lambda x+y-2=0, \lambda x+\lambda y+3=0\) is consistent, then
questions.solution:
The system of equations will be consistent if
\(\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & \lambda & 2 \\
\lambda & 1 & -2 \\
\lambda & \lambda & 3
\end{array}\right|=0\)
To evaluate \(\Delta\) we use \(R_1 \rightarrow R_1+R_2\) followed by \(\mathrm{C}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_2-\mathrm{C}_1\) to obtain
\(\begin{aligned}
\Delta & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\lambda+1 & \lambda+1 & 0 \\
\lambda & 1 & -2 \\
\lambda & \lambda & 3
\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\lambda+1 & 0 & 0 \\
\lambda & 1-\lambda & -2 \\
\lambda & 0 & 3
\end{array}\right| \\
& =3(\lambda+1)(1-\lambda)=3\left(1-\lambda^2\right)
\end{aligned}\)
For the system to be consistent, we must have \(1-\lambda^2=0\) or \(\lambda= \pm 1\).

questions.solution:
Let the persons be \(\mathrm{A}\) and \(\mathrm{B}\).
Suppose that A has the first throw. We know that the probability of getting 'a three' in a single throw \(=\frac{1}{6}\) and that of 'not getting a three'
\(=1-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{6} \text {. }\)
\(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A}\) wins \()=\frac{1}{6}+\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 \frac{1}{6}+\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4 \frac{1}{6}+\ldots\). .to \(\infty\)
[Since, A can win at the \(1^{\text {st }}, 3^{\text {rd }}, 5^{\text {th }}, \ldots\). mutually exclusive trials with respective probabilities
\(\begin{aligned}
& \left.\frac{1}{6},\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 \frac{1}{6},\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4 \frac{1}{6} \ldots \ldots\right] \\
& =\frac{1}{6}\left[1+\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2+\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2+\ldots \ldots . .\right] \\
& =\frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{1-\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2}=\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{36}{36-25}=\frac{6}{11} \\
& \Rightarrow P(\text { Bwins })=1-\frac{6}{11}=\frac{5}{11} .
\end{aligned}\)
i.e. the probability of winning of the person having the first throw \(=\frac{6}{11}\) and that of the other \(=\frac{5}{11}\).
Hence the ratio of chances of their winning = 6:5.

questions.q: n the set \(\mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N}\), the relation \(\mathrm{R}\) is defined by (a, b) \(R(c, d) \Leftrightarrow a d=b c\). Then \(R\) is
options: reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
questions.solution:
The relation is defined on \(\mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N}\). since the elements of \(\mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N}\) are ordered pairs hence the relation on \(\mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N}\) relates two ordered pairs. Now,
(1) \(\forall \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b} \in \mathbf{N} \quad \mathrm{ab}=\mathrm{ba}\)
\(\therefore(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}) \mathrm{R}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}) \forall(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}) \in \mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N}\). Thus \(\mathrm{R}\) is refiexive
(ii) Let
\(\begin{aligned}
& (a, b) R(c, d) \Leftrightarrow a d=b c \forall(a, b) \text { and }(c, d) \in N \times N \\
& \Rightarrow b c=a d \Rightarrow c b=d a \Rightarrow(c, d) R(a, b) .
\end{aligned}\)
Thus \(R\) is symmetric
(iii) Again let (a,b) R (c,d) and (c,d) R (e,f)
\(\Rightarrow \mathrm{ad}=\mathrm{bc}\) and \(\mathrm{cf}=\mathrm{de}\)
\(\Rightarrow\) adcf \(=\) bcde \(\Rightarrow\) af \(=\) de \(\Rightarrow(a, b) R(e, f)\)
Thus \(\mathrm{R}\) is transitive.
Thus \(\mathrm{R}\) is equivalence relation.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the line passing through \((1,2,3)\) and parallel to the planes \(r \cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2 \hat{k})=5\) and r. \((3 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=6\) is
questions.solution:
The equation of line passing through \((1,2\),
3) and parallel to \(b\) is given by
\(r=(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})+\lambda\left(b_1 \hat{i}+b_2 \hat{j}+b_3 \hat{k}\right)\) ...(i)
The equations of the given planes are
\(\begin{aligned}
& r \cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2 \hat{k})=5 \quad ...(ii)\\
& \text { and } r \cdot(3 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=6 \quad ...(iii)
\end{aligned}\)
The line in eq. (i) and plane in eq. (ii) are parallel. Therefore, the normal to the plane of eq. (ii) and the given line are perpendicular.
\(\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2 \hat{k}) \cdot \lambda\left(b_1 \hat{i}+b_2 \hat{j}+b_3 \hat{k}\right)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \lambda\left(b_1-b_2+2 b_3\right)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad\left(b_1-b_2+2 b_3\right)=0 \quad ...(iv)
\end{aligned}\)
Similarly,
\(\begin{aligned}
& (3 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \cdot \lambda\left(b_1 \hat{i}+b_2 \hat{j}+b_3 \hat{k}\right)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \lambda\left(3 b_1+b_2+b_3\right)=0 \quad ...(v)
\end{aligned}\)
From eqs. (iv) and (v), we obtain
\(\begin{aligned}
& \frac{b_1}{(-1) \times 1-1 \times 2}=\frac{b_2}{2 \times 3-1 \times 1}=\frac{b_3}{1 \times 1-3(-1)} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{b_1}{-3}=\frac{b_2}{5}=\frac{b_3}{4}
\end{aligned}\)
Therefore, the direction ratios of \(b\) are \(-3,5\) and 4 .
\(\therefore \mathrm{b}=\mathrm{b}_1 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\mathrm{b}_2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\mathrm{b}_3 \hat{\mathrm{k}}=-3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+5 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+4 \hat{\mathrm{k}}\)
Substituting the value of \(b\) in eq. (i), we obtain
\(r=(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})+\lambda(-3 \hat{i}+5 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k})\)
This is the equation of the required line.

questions.q: A sphere of constant radius \(2 \mathrm{k}\) passes through the origin and meets the axes in A, B, C. The locus of the centroid of the tetrahedron \(\mathrm{OABC}\) is
questions.solution:
Let co-ordinate of the points A, B, C be \((\mathrm{a}, 0,0),(0, \mathrm{~b}, 0)\) and \((0,0, \mathrm{c})\) respectively. Then equation of the sphere \(\mathrm{OABC}\) is
\(x^2+y^2+z^2-a x-b y-c z=0\)
Radius of this sphere is equal to \(2 \mathrm{k}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2+\mathrm{c}^2=4(2 \mathrm{k})^2=16 \mathrm{k}^2\)
Also let (z,y, z) be the co-ordinates of the centroid of the tetrahedron \(\mathrm{OABC}\), then
\(\mathrm{x}=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y}=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{~b}, \mathrm{z}=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{c}\)
so that \(\mathrm{a}=4 \mathrm{x}, \mathrm{b}=4 \mathrm{y}, \mathrm{c}=4 \mathrm{z}\)
Eliminating a, b, c from (1) and (2), the required locus is
\(\begin{aligned}
& 16 x^2+16 y^2+16 z^2=16 k^2 \\
& \text { or } x^2+y^2+z^2=k^2
\end{aligned}\)

questions.q: If \(2 y \cos \theta=x \sin \theta\) and \(2 x \sec \theta-y \operatorname{cosec} \theta=3\), then \(x^2+4 y^2=\)
questions.solution:
We have \(2 \mathrm{y} \cos \theta=\mathrm{x} \sin \theta\)
or \(\frac{\cos \theta}{\mathrm{x}}=\frac{\sin \theta}{2 \mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{k}\) (say)
Then \(\cos \theta=\mathrm{kx}\) and \(\sin \theta=2 \mathrm{ky}\) ...(1)
Again \(2 \mathrm{x} \sec \theta-\mathrm{y} \operatorname{cosec} \theta=3\)
or \(\frac{2 \mathrm{x}}{\cos \theta}-\frac{\mathrm{y}}{\sin \theta}=3\)
or \(\frac{2 \mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{kx}}-\frac{\mathrm{y}}{2 \mathrm{ky}}=3 \quad\) [from(1)]
or \(\frac{2}{\mathrm{k}}-\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{k}}=3\), giving \(\mathrm{k}=\frac{1}{2}\)
We now get \(\cos \theta=\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2}\) and \(\sin \theta=\mathrm{y}\)
Squaring and adding we get
\(\begin{aligned}
& \cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta=\frac{x^2}{4+y^2} \\

questions.solution: The four points are \(P(-2,3,4), Q(-4,4,6), R(4\), \(3,5), \mathrm{S}(0,1,2)\). \(\therefore\) direction ratios of RS are \(0-4,1-3,2-5\), i.e., \(4,2,3\). Dividing each by \(\sqrt{(4)^2+(2)^2+(3)^2}\), i.e., \(\sqrt{29}\), the actual direction cosines' of RS are \(\frac{4}{\sqrt{29}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}, \frac{3}{\sqrt{29}} \text {. }\) \(\therefore\) Projection of \(\mathrm{PQ}\) on \(\mathrm{RS}\) \(\begin{aligned} & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{29}}(-4+2)+\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}(4-3)+\frac{3}{\sqrt{29}}(6-4) \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{29}}(-8+2+6)=0 \end{aligned}\) which implies that \(\mathrm{PQ} \perp \mathrm{RS}\)

It is given that \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \times(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}})=\frac{1}{2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}\)
Note: \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \times(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}})=(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}) \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}-(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}) \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}\)
\(\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}=(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}) \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}-(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}) \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}-\frac{1}{2}\right) \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}-(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}) \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}=0 \quad ...(i)
\end{aligned}\)
Since \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{c}\) are non-parallel, therefore for the existence of relation (i), the coeff. of \(\bar{b}\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{c}}\) should vanish separately. Therefore, we get \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}-\frac{1}{2}=0\) i.e., \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}=0\) Since \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}\) are the unit vectors therefore
\(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{3} \cdot\left(\because \cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\theta\right)\)

questions.q: In the network shown in the Fig, each resistance is \(1 \Omega\). The effective resistance between \(A\) and \(B\) is
questions.solution:
At A current is distributed and at B currents are collected. Between A and B, the distribution is symmetrical. It has been shown in the figure. It appears that current in \(\mathrm{AO}\) and \(\mathrm{OB}\) remains same. At \(\mathrm{O}\), current \(\mathrm{i}_4\) returns back without any change. If we detach \(\mathrm{O}\) from \(\mathrm{AB}\) there will not be any change in distribution. Now, CO & OD will be in series hence its total resistance \(=2 \Omega\) It is in parallel with \(\mathrm{CD}\), so, equivalent resistance \(=\frac{2 \times 1}{2+1}=\frac{2}{3} \Omega\) This equivalent resistance is in series with \(\mathrm{AC}\) & \(\mathrm{DB}\), so, total resistance \(=\frac{2}{3}+1+1=\frac{8}{3} \Omega\)
Now \(\frac{8}{3} \Omega\) is parallel to \(\mathrm{AB}\), that is, \(2 \Omega\), so total resistance \(=\frac{8 / 3 \times 2}{8 / 3+2}=\frac{16 / 3}{14 / 3}=\frac{16}{14}=\frac{8}{7} \Omega\) [Alt:
Between \(\mathrm{C}\) & D, the equivalent resistance is given by \(1 / \mathrm{r}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}_3}+\frac{1}{\left(\mathrm{r}_4+\mathrm{r}_5\right)}=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\) Equivalent resistance along \(\mathrm{ACDB}=1+\frac{2}{3}+1=\frac{8}{3}\) \(\therefore\) Effective resistance between \(\mathrm{A}\) and \(\mathrm{B}\) is \(\left.\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{7}{8} \text { or } \mathrm{R}=\frac{8}{7}\right]\)

\end{aligned}\)

(According to de-Broglie, wavelength associated with an electron \(\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{mv}}\))
